query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a cryogenic rolling process immediately followed by an optimized low‐temperature annealing treatment will refine the dual-phase lamellar colonies in eutectic high‐entropy alloys by forming a homogeneous distribution of coherent nano-scale L12 precipitates within the ductile FCC lamellae. This refined microstructure is expected to reduce stress concentrations at the numerous internal boundaries, thereby simultaneously enhancing yield strength and room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the conventional processing route.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventionally processed eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting dual-phase lamellar colonies, where numerous internal boundaries promote microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Apply a cryogenic rolling process followed by an optimized low-temperature annealing treatment designed to induce the formation of coherent nano-scale L12 precipitates within the lamellae.
generation.conditions: Ambient (room-temperature) tensile deformation tests on alloy specimens processed via the proposed combined deformation–annealing route versus specimens processed by conventional methods.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, hierarchical nano-lamellar microstructure with a uniform distribution of finely dispersed, coherent L12 precipitates embedded in the ductile FCC phase.
generation.mechanism: The cryogenic rolling introduces a high density of defects and refines the lamellar structure, while the subsequent low-temperature annealing facilitates controlled precipitation of L12 phases. These nano-scale precipitates strengthen the alloy via dislocation bypass mechanisms and help homogenize strain distribution at internal boundaries, thus mitigating the stress concentrations that lead to microcracking.
generation.predicted_outcome: An improvement in both yield strength and tensile ductility is expected, with enhanced work hardening behavior and delayed onset of microcrack formation compared to the baseline material processed conventionally.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloy processed using conventional techniques, characterized by dual-phase lamellar colonies with internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation under room-temperature tensile loading.
generation.boundary: This beneficial effect is expected when the alloy chemistry and initial lamellar spacing allow for effective cryogenic deformation and subsequent precipitation without overrefinement or formation of deleterious brittle phases. Excessive interstitial contamination or non-optimal annealing parameters may suppress the desired precipitate formation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact processing parameters such as the magnitude of cryogenic strain, annealing temperature, and time require optimization for different alloy compositions within the eutectic high-entropy alloy family. The quantitative improvement in strength and ductility remains to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens of a eutectic high-entropy alloy. One set will undergo the cryogenic rolling followed by optimized low-temperature annealing, while the control set will be processed via the conventional route. Perform room-temperature tensile tests and use microscopy (TEM, EBSD) to analyze the microstructure and precipitate distribution.
measurements: Microstructural features (grain size, precipitate size/distribution, and internal boundary morphology)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the processed specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in both yield strength and tensile ductility compared with the conventionally processed baseline, or if microcrack density is not reduced (or is increased) despite the intervention.

Enhanced strength and ductility in a friction stir processing engineered dual phase high entropy alloy

Abstract: AbstractThe potential of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) to exhibit an extraordinary combination of properties by shifting the compositional regime from the corners towards the centers of phase diagrams has led to worldwide attention by material scientists. Here we present a strong and ductile non-equiatomic HEA obtained after friction stir processing (FSP). A transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) assisted HEA with composition Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 (at.%) was severely deformed by FSP and evaluated for its microstructure-mechanical property relationship. The FSP-engineered microstructure of the TRIP HEA exhibited a substantially smaller grain size, and optimized fractions of face-centered cubic (f.c.c., γ) and hexagonal close-packed (h.c.p., ε) phases, as compared to the as-homogenized reference material. This results in synergistic strengthening via TRIP, grain boundary strengthening, and effective strain partitioning between the γ and ε phases during deformation, thus leading to enhanced strength and ductility of the TRIP-assisted dual-phase HEA engineered via FSP.

Simultaneous Strength-Ductility Enhancement of a Nano-Lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High Entropy Alloy by Cryo-Rolling and Annealing

Abstract: Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. Influence of ordered L12 precipitation on strain-rate dependent mechanical behavior in a eutectic high entropy alloy

Abstract: Recent studies indicate that eutectic high-entropy alloys can simultaneously possess high strength and high ductility, which have potential industrial applications. The present study focuses on Al0.7CoCrFeNi, a lamellar dual-phase (fcc + B2) precipitation-strengthenable eutectic high entropy alloy. This alloy exhibits an fcc + B2 (B2 with bcc nano-precipitates) microstructure resulting in a combination of the soft and ductile fcc phase together with hard B2 phase. Low temperature annealing leads to the precipitation of ordered L12 intermetallic precipitates within the fcc resulting in enhanced strength. The strengthening contribution due to fine scale L12 is modeled using Orowan dislocation bowing and by-pass mechanism. The alloy was tested under quasi-static (strain-rate = 10−3 s−1) tensile loading and dynamic (strain-rate = 103 s−1) compressive loading.
